1. Problem Statement
Large Language Models (LLMs) can assist in analyzing financial statements, but the
quality of their responses depends heavily on how they are prompted. There is
limited practical guidance on which prompting strategies produce the most
accurate, complete, and reliable financial analyses. This project aims to evaluate
different prompting techniques to identify the most effective approach for financial
statement analysis.
Relevance
Prompt engineering is a fundamental aspect of LLM engineering because the quality
of an LLM's output is directly influenced by the prompt design. In financial
applications, inaccurate or incomplete responses can lead to incorrect interpretations
of financial information. Evaluating different prompting strategies helps improve the
reliability and consistency of LLM-based financial analysis while providing practical
insights for real-world business applications.
Domain
Prompt Engineering
LLM Evaluation
Financial Document Understanding
LLM Applications
Risks & Fallback
Technical Risk: Financial statements often contain complex tables and PDF layouts
that may result in incorrect text extraction, affecting the quality of the LLM's
analysis.
Fallback Plan: If PDF extraction proves unreliable, the project will use clean text or
CSV versions of the same financial statements. The evaluation of prompting
strategies will remain unchanged, allowing the core objectives of the project to be
completed successfully.
2. Proposed Approach

The proposed system will accept financial statements (Balance Sheet and Income
Statement) in PDF format, extract the relevant text and financial information, and
analyze them using a Large Language Model (LLM). Our system will evaluate 4
different prompting strategies for financial statement analysis using the Large
Language Model (LLM).
The strategies include
1. Basic Prompting, where the model is asked to analyze the financial statement
directly.
2. Role-Based Prompting, where the model is instructed to act as an experienced
CPA/CA or financial analyst.
3. Structured Prompting, where the model is guided to produce a predefined
analysis covering key financial metrics such as revenue, expenses, profitability,
financial ratios, and potential risks.
4. Few-Shot Prompting, where the model is first provided with an example financial
statement analysis before analyzing a new financial statement. The outputs from
each prompting strategy will be compared using evaluation metrics such as
accuracy, completeness, hallucination rate, and response time to determine the
most effective prompting technique for financial statement analysis.
Project Type
Working Demo + Experimental Evaluation
This project will include a functional web application for financial statement
analysis and an experimental comparison of different prompting strategies using the
same LLM.
Models
Primary Model
Gemini 2.5 Flash
Optional Comparison Model (if required)
GPT-4.1 mini or Llama 3.1 8B Instruct
The primary evaluation will use Gemini 2.5 Flash to ensure a consistent comparison
across prompting strategies.

Datasets / Benchmarks
The project will use:
Publicly available financial statements
Sample balance sheets and income statements from accounting education
resources.
A small manually created evaluation dataset (10–20 financial statements) with
expected outputs for comparison.
Tools / Frameworks
Python 3.11
Streamlit
Gemini API
pdfplumber (or PyMuPDF) for PDF text extraction
pandas for data processing
Matplotlib for result visualization
Jupyter Notebook for experiments
What is Novel?
Most existing financial document applications use a single prompting approach
without evaluating its effectiveness. This project systematically compares multiple
prompting strategies on the same financial statements using quantitative evaluation
metrics such as accuracy, completeness, hallucination rate, and response time to
identify the most effective prompt design.
Compute Budget
The development will be performed on a standard laptop (8–16 GB RAM) using
Python and Streamlit. LLM inference will be provided through the Gemini API,
eliminating the need for dedicated GPU hardware. Google Colab (Free Tier) may be
used for experimentation and evaluation if needed.
3. Related Work
The proposed project builds upon existing research in financial language models,

prompt engineering, and LLM-based document understanding. Previous studies
have focused on developing domain-specific financial LLMs or improving financial
question answering. However, limited work has systematically evaluated how
different prompting strategies influence the quality of financial statement analysis
using general-purpose LLMs. This project addresses that gap by comparing multiple
prompting techniques and measuring their effectiveness using objective evaluation
metrics.
Reference (Title, Authors, Year)
I. BloombergGPT: A Large Language Model for Finance – Wu et al., 2023
BloombergGPT introduces a finance-specific LLM trained on financial data. In
contrast, this project evaluates how prompt engineering can improve financial
statement analysis using a general-purpose LLM without additional model training.
II. FinGPT: Open-Source Financial Large Language Models – Yang et al., 2023
FinGPT focuses on developing and fine-tuning open-source financial language
models. This project instead compares multiple prompting strategies to improve
analysis quality while using an existing LLM through an API.
III. Prompt Engineering Guide – Lee Boonstra, Google, 2024
The Prompt Engineering Guide describes various prompting techniques for LLMs.
This project applies and experimentally evaluates those techniques in the financial
statement analysis domain using quantitative performance metrics.
4. Expected Deliverables
Code Repository
PDF/text extraction scripts
Prompt templates
Financial analysis engine
Streamlit web application
Evaluation scripts
README with setup instructions

Report
Literature review
Methodology
Prompt designs
Experimental setup
Results and analysis
Limitations
Future work
Demo
A Streamlit application where the user will be able to perform below task.
I. Uploads a financial statement.
ii. Selects a prompting strategy.
iii. Generates the analysis.
iv. Compares the outputs.
5. Evaluation Plan
• Metric Baseline Target
• Financial fact extraction accuracy Basic prompt: 75% Structured prompt:
≥90%
• Summary completeness Basic prompt: 70% Structured prompt: ≥90%
• Hallucination rate 15% <5%
• Response time 8 seconds <5 seconds
• User rating (1–5) 3.5 ≥4.5
prompt:
You will analyze a financial statement. First study the example:
an example statement followed by the ideal analysis. Then produce
an analysis of the same quality, depth, and format for the target
statement.

=== EXAMPLE FINANCIAL STATEMENT ===
Example Manufacturing Co. - Fiscal Year 2023 (USD millions)

Income Statement                    FY2023    FY2022
Revenue                              500.0     450.0
Cost of goods sold                  (300.0)   (275.0)
Gross profit                         200.0     175.0
Operating expenses                  (120.0)   (110.0)
Operating income                      80.0      65.0
Interest expense                     (10.0)     (8.0)
Income before taxes                   70.0      57.0
Income tax expense (21%)             (14.7)    (12.0)
Net income                            55.3      45.0

Balance Sheet (at year end)
Cash and equivalents                  40.0      35.0
Accounts receivable                   60.0      52.0
Inventory                             50.0      41.0
Total current assets                 150.0     128.0
Total assets                         400.0     360.0
Total current liabilities             75.0      70.0
Long-term debt                       130.0     120.0
Total liabilities                    220.0     205.0
Shareholders' equity                 180.0     155.0

=== IDEAL ANALYSIS ===
Executive Summary: Example Manufacturing delivered a strong FY2023.
Revenue grew 11.1% to $500.0M and net income rose 22.9% to $55.3M,
outpacing sales growth thanks to operating leverage. The balance
sheet remains healthy, with liquidity comfortably above 2x current
obligations, though inventory growth and rising debt deserve watch.

Revenue: Revenue increased $50.0M (11.1%) year over year to $500.0M,
indicating solid demand.

Expenses: COGS rose 9.1% to $300.0M, slower than revenue, lifting
gross margin to 40.0% (FY2022: 38.9%). Operating expenses grew 9.1%
to $120.0M, so operating income improved to $80.0M (16.0% margin).

Profitability: Net income of $55.3M yields an 11.1% net margin
(FY2022: 10.0%). Return on equity is 30.7% ($55.3M / $180.0M),
exceptional profitability on the shareholders' capital base.

Liquidity: Current ratio is 2.0 ($150.0M / $75.0M) and quick ratio
is 1.33 (($150.0M - $50.0M) / $75.0M) - both comfortable. Note
inventory grew 22.0%, faster than sales; monitor for obsolescence.

Solvency: Debt-to-equity is 1.22 ($220.0M / $180.0M). Interest
coverage is 8.0x ($80.0M / $10.0M), so debt service is well
supported, but long-term debt rose $10.0M during the year.

Financial Ratios: Gross margin 40.0%; operating margin 16.0%; net
margin 11.1%; current ratio 2.0; quick ratio 1.33; debt-to-equity
1.22; interest coverage 8.0x; ROE 30.7%.

Risks: (1) Inventory build-up (+22.0% vs +11.1% sales) risks
write-downs if demand softens. (2) Rising leverage - long-term debt
up 8.3% - increases interest burden in a rising-rate environment.
(3) Receivables growth (15.4%) slightly ahead of sales may signal
loosening credit terms.

Recommendations: (1) Tighten inventory management toward FY2022
turnover levels to release working capital. (2) Use part of the
$40.0M cash balance to pay down long-term debt and hold
debt-to-equity below 1.2. (3) Formalize receivables collection
targets to keep DSO from expanding.

Utilizing Gemini 2.5 Flash and a Streamlit-based web application, the project aims to compare basic, role-based, structured, and few-shot prompting techniques across accuracy, completeness, hallucination rate, and response time metrics. While the project presents a clear methodology and strong practical relevance, technical risks regarding PDF text extraction require reliable fallback mechanisms.

Revenue: Revenue is not reported in the provided project document, as this document represents a technical research proposal rather than a corporate financial statement.

Expenses: Operating and capital expenses are not reported in the provided project document, though the project operates under a constrained compute budget relying primarily on standard local hardware and API-based inference costs.

Profitability: Net profit metrics are not reported since the target text is a software development and research proposal rather than a corporate income statement. 

Liquidity: Liquidity metrics are not reported as the document lacks a corporate balance sheet. However, resource allocation relies on a standard laptop (8-16 GB RAM) and the Gemini API, requiring minimal capital expenditure.

Solvency: Solvency metrics, including debt-to-equity and interest coverage, are not reported because the document is a technical project proposal rather than a corporate financial statement.

Financial Ratios: Gross margin not reported; operating margin not reported; net margin not reported; current ratio not reported; quick ratio not reported; debt-to-equity not reported; interest coverage not reported; ROE not reported.

Risks: (1) Technical risk of complex financial table and PDF layouts resulting in incorrect text extraction and affecting LLM analysis quality. (2) Potential variability in LLM outputs across different prompting strategies affecting accuracy and completeness. (3) Reliance on external API stability (Gemini API) for system performance during evaluation.

Recommendations: (1) Implement the fallback plan utilizing clean text or CSV versions of financial statements if PDF extraction proves unreliable. (2) Maintain consistent evaluation baselines using Gemini 2.5 Flash as the primary model across all four prompting strategies. (3) Utilize the proposed evaluation dataset of 10-20 manually created financial statements to rigorously track accuracy, hallucination rates, and response times.
